You hold momentum with warmth, and that same steadiness is what lets you sit with something unanswered instead of closing it early. The fire stays lit around you partly because you can imagine what hasn't happened yet without needing it resolved first.

The whole shape of things is available to you. You can see how the pieces fit, which means you are free to imagine a piece turning out another way. Picture that going differently than it sits now, hold it that way for a minute, and take one small step in that direction before the week is out. Nothing has to be settled. You are only finding out what it looks like when you move.
1.sheetLine: You can picture what hasn't happened and walk toward it.

2.tense: You are already bracing for a future you cannot write in advance, and that bracing has taken the pen.
2.verb: tending the fire
2.place: standing back far enough to see the whole of it
2.ask: Whatever you've been holding back for fear of how it lands — say it plainly, kindly, once. Then let it stand without checking whether it was received.
2.core:
You tend the fire well enough that you can read how the pieces fit together, and right now that reading has turned into guarding. You have started lining up what might happen, calibrating your words before you speak, running the conversation ahead of time. The warmth that usually moves people forward is on hold while you prepare for every possibility at once.

You can say a hard thing without it becoming a weapon. Whatever you are carrying that somebody needs to hear, say it plainly, once, with care for how it lands. Then leave it alone. Hold your clarity steady instead of refreshing it. Some of what you are bracing for won't happen, and what you said will already have said it.
2.sheetLine: Bracing for every future keeps the fire from warming anyone.

3.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed in front of you, watching a pattern that already moved on.
3.verb: tending the fire
3.place: standing back far enough to see the whole of it
3.ask: A role, a plan, a way of showing up has finished. Let it be done, keep only the part still worth carrying, and do the next thing that only works once it's over.
3.core:
You know how to keep a fire going and you can read how things connect, but that reading is pointed backward now. You keep revisiting what already happened, holding the shape of it, because that is easier than looking at what a next thing would need. The fire is banked. There is still heat, but nothing new is catching.

Something you are still tending has already finished. Say what it is, let it be finished, and keep only the part of it that still serves you. Then do the next thing that only makes sense if the finished thing is over. You don't have to want the new thing yet. You only have to stop warming the old one.
3.sheetLine: You keep warming something that has already gone out.

4.tense: The pen is down, but you are already writing the next chapter of the room.
4.verb: tending the fire
4.place: standing back far enough to see the whole of it
4.ask: A change you keep seeing is overdue — make one small unglamorous action toward it this week. No announcement, no permission. Just the first real inch.
4.core:
You can read how the whole pattern fits, and you keep moving things forward, but you aren't naming that movement as yours. The changes you bring get filed under circumstance, good timing, or someone else's suggestion. You notice what is overdue and then act on it without ever writing your own name on what you saw.

A change you keep seeing should happen. Take one real inch of it this week, a small unglamorous action that only makes sense if you are building it. No announcement. The inch is the point. When it is done, see that you did it, and mark it somewhere you'll find it again.
4.sheetLine: The change you keep seeing is already yours.

1.tense: A build is on its last step and you are holding it there while it finishes.
1.verb: tending the fire under something so it can finish and open into the next
1.place: the step where a build is finally whole and only now gives way to what comes next
1.ask: Give an afternoon to picturing what follows a piece of work that's done, then take the first small step toward it.
1.core: You keep a thing going past the interesting part, when others have drifted off, and that is a real skill. Keeping it also means setting down what's done. An ending here isn't a wall, it's a door, and your even hand is what gets people across the sill. The whole build is close, and something in you can already picture the next plot of ground. That picture is yours, but it only becomes real if you move toward it. So give an afternoon to imagining what follows — what it looks like, who's in it — and take the first small step that way. The hard part is already behind you. The next step is lighter because your own hand is the one pointing at it.
1.sheetLine: What you kept going is done, so walk through the open door.

2.tense: Where a thing is meant to be finished, you will be pushing it past its own edge.
2.verb: tending the fire under something so it can finish and open into the next
2.place: the step where a build is finally whole and only now gives way to what comes next
2.ask: Say one true thing plainly to someone you're holding up, without softening it, and tend nothing after it for a week.
2.core: You keep momentum alive in the ones near you, and that has earned trust. When it runs hot, holding someone up turns into pushing: you can feel a thing near its end and add fuel anyway, because watching it sit finished feels like dropping it. So the person who needs a plain word from you keeps getting hints instead. You're bracing at a future you can't write by force. The outcome sits behind a door they have to open, and fuel won't open it for them. Say one hard thing once — gently, plainly — and then nothing. If this read is wrong and nobody was braced, no damage is done: they heard something true from someone who carries weight. The quiet you're dodging is smaller than the collapse you're racing.
2.sheetLine: You're feeding a fire that's already done burning.

3.tense: Where a thing could be finished, it stays open behind you while the fire runs low.
3.verb: tending the fire under something so it can finish and open into the next
3.place: the step where a build is finally whole and only now gives way to what comes next
3.ask: Hold one lingering thing untouched for three days, then finish it for good in a single clear evening.
3.core: Somewhere in you the one who keeps the fire going hasn't shown up in a while, and whatever that's about belongs to your life, not to this draw. What's visible is the build stuck on its last step, something left open that could have closed, and the fuel it takes to stand in that doorway. Nobody can order you to want it again. What's left is smaller than wanting. Hold one lingering thing untouched for three days, then finish it in a single clear evening. The things you hold onto sit better when the ones you're through with are gone. That's the whole ask for now. If it turns out to be the wrong room, you've cleared an evening and found out which one is right.
3.sheetLine: The door's stood open a while, so close one thing tonight.

4.tense: You are carrying changes through to the end and telling the room you're undecided.
4.verb: tending the fire under something so it can finish and open into the next
4.place: the step where a build is finally whole and only now gives way to what comes next
4.ask: Move one piece of a change you've already settled on — an email, a shelf, a bag heading out the door — and don't announce it as a decision.
4.core: Finished things near you cross the line while you describe yourself as someone who hasn't chosen. Someone has to steady the middle of a project, hold the plan when others change course, take the keys at the end — that work is happening through you, and it doesn't make the cut of the story you tell about yourself. The story says drifting. The ones moving alongside you say something else. So here's the ask, small and plain: move one piece of a change you've already made up your mind about. One shelf cleared, one bag carried out, one message sent. It doesn't need to be announced. If the read misses, you've improved one shelf and seen who was standing close. The shift was yours. Letting it be named yours can come later, and in the simplest shape first.
4.sheetLine: You're handing things over while saying you haven't chosen.
